name: Crater Rim Scramble (from Easton Glacier)
approach: Start at the Park Butte Trailhead (elev. ~3,360 ft) at the end of Forest Service Road 13, reached via the Baker Lake Highway/Sulfur Creek Road turnoff (do not repeat the drive-in here — this covers the hike only). From the trailhead register, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. Within the first 0.3–0.4 mile the trail fords Sulfur Creek — a braided, silty glacial-melt crossing that can run high and fast on warm afternoons; it's usually rock-hoppable or bridged by a seasonal log/plank in early summer but worth checking current Forest Service trail-condition notes before a hot-day crossing. Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche-path terrain, crosses a couple of additional meltwater streams, then switchbacks up a forested slope into Morovitz Meadows (~2 miles in). At the upper meadow, bear right at the signed junction with the Scott Paul Trail #603.1 (which splits left) to stay on Park Butte Trail, then take the next right fork onto the Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass/the glacier (straight ahead leads to the Park Butte lookout instead). Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 climbs onto the crest of a narrow lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a distinctive, uniformly graded ridge (hence the name) with exposed, steep drop-offs on both sides in places; use care in wind or on icy/frosty mornings. Designated Railroad Grade camps sit at 2.25–2.75 miles from the trailhead; High Camp sites are at about 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp, at roughly 5,900 ft, marks the end of maintained tread. From Sandy Camp the route continues cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier, typically 3–4 hours car-to-camp for most parties. Rope up for glacier travel around 6,800–7,200 ft (conditions-dependent) and ascend the Easton Glacier heading north, angling slightly west toward Sherman Peak; the standard line stays east (climber's right) of the glacier's major crevasse bands, though route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the approach and shifts season to season — wanding the route is standard practice given frequent whiteout/cloud cap conditions on Baker's south side. Above roughly 9,600–9,800 ft the route skirts the rim of Sherman Crater, where active fumaroles vent sulfurous steam (occasionally noticeable by smell and visible venting) — stay on the established boot path here and keep gear away from the acidic, degraded rock near the vents. No potable water exists at the trailhead itself; plan on treating water from Sulfur/Rocky Creek near the start or from snowmelt at High/Sandy Camp.

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail and the Railroad Grade moraine to Sandy Camp, then the Easton Glacier to the crater rim
approach_variants.notes:
From the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of FR-13 near 3,360 ft, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. Within the first 0.3-0.4 mile the trail fords Sulfur Creek — braided, silty glacial melt that runs high and fast on warm afternoons, usually rock-hoppable or bridged by a seasonal plank early in the summer.

Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche terrain, crosses more meltwater streams, and switchbacks into Morovitz Meadows about two miles in. At the upper meadow bear right at the signed Scott Paul Trail #603.1 junction to stay on Park Butte, then take the next right onto Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass. Straight ahead at that second fork goes to the Park Butte lookout instead — a pleasant hike and the wrong one.

Railroad Grade #603.2 climbs onto the crest of the lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a uniformly graded ridge, hence the name, with steep drops on both sides in places. Designated camps sit at 2.25-2.75 miles; High Camp is around 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft is where maintained tread ends.

There is no potable water at the trailhead. Treat from Sulfur or Rocky Creek near the start, or melt at camp.
hazards: A braided glacial ford of Sulfur Creek that runs high on warm afternoons
Exposed drops on both sides of the Railroad Grade moraine crest, worse in wind or on frosty mornings
A crevasse field that is the technical crux of the approach and moves season to season
Baker's characteristic cloud cap and whiteouts on the south side, above the last natural handrail
Active fumaroles and acid-degraded rock at the Sherman Crater rim
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The moraine crest is a handrail you can follow blind, and Sandy Camp is where it ends. Railroad Grade is exactly what its name says: a narrow, uniformly graded spine with the drop on both sides. In whiteout — which is the normal condition on Baker's south side, where a cloud cap forms on otherwise clear days — you do not navigate on this stretch, you follow the spine. When the maintained tread stops at Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft, you are at the end of the handrail and the start of the route.

From there the route is cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier. Rope up somewhere around 6,800-7,200 ft depending on conditions. The glacier heading is north, angling slightly west toward Sherman Peak, and the standard line stays east — climber's right — of the glacier's major crevasse bands.

Wand it. This is not a hedge; it is standard practice on this route precisely because the crater rim and the moraine crest offer no natural handrail above Sandy Camp and the cloud cap arrives without warning. Route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the whole approach and it shifts season to season, so your own wands going up are the only reliable line coming down.

Arrival at Sherman Peak itself: above roughly 9,600-9,800 ft you reach the rim of Sherman Crater, and you will smell it before you see it — active fumaroles vent sulphurous steam, and the rock near them is acid-degraded. That smell is the confirmation that you are at the crater rim and not on the Roman Wall heading for Baker's true summit, which is the other thing this glacier leads to. Stay on the established boot path here and keep gear off the degraded rock.

What going too far looks like: continuing up past the crater rim onto the steep sustained snow of the Roman Wall means you have left Sherman Peak below you and are climbing Mount Baker.
